opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important open questions right now, because a lot of our existing benchmarks were designed for a very different kind of model. They're largely single-turn: you give the model a question, it produces an answer, and you check whether that answer matches a reference. That made sense when we were measuring knowledge or reasoning in isolation. But agentic models are doing something fundamentally different. They're taking sequences of actions over long horizons, interacting with an environment, calling tools, recovering from mistakes, and the final answer is often just the tip of the iceberg.

So the first thing I'd say is that benchmarks need to move toward evaluating trajectories, not just outcomes. If an agent gets the right result but took fifty unnecessary steps, or got lucky after a series of bad decisions, that tells you something very different than an agent that planned well and executed cleanly. Conversely, an agent might fail the final task but show really strong intermediate behavior, like correctly identifying that it lacked information and asking for it. Pass/fail on the end state loses a lot of that signal.

The second piece is realism of the environment. A lot of agentic benchmarks today are fairly sandboxed: clean APIs, deterministic responses, well-specified tasks. Real-world tasks are messy. Instructions are ambiguous, tools fail, web pages change, and the user may not know exactly what they want. I think we need benchmarks that deliberately inject that kind of noise and measure robustness: how does the agent handle a tool returning an error, or conflicting information from two sources? That's where you really see the gap between a demo and something you'd actually deploy.

Third, long-horizon capability. Many of the tasks people actually want agents for, like doing a multi-day research project, managing a codebase change across many files, or coordinating a workflow, unfold over hours or longer. Most benchmarks top out at tasks a human could do in a few minutes. Measuring how performance degrades as task length grows, and whether the model can maintain coherent state and goals over that time, is critical. Some recent work framing capability in terms of the length of tasks agents can complete reliably is a really useful lens there.

I'd also add reliability and consistency as first-class metrics. For agents, it's not enough to succeed once out of five tries. If you're going to hand off a real task, you need to know it'll succeed nearly every time, so metrics that capture consistency across runs, rather than best-of-k, matter a lot more in the agentic setting.

And finally, cost and efficiency. Agents can burn through a lot of compute, tokens, and tool calls. Two agents with the same success rate can be wildly different in practical value if one costs ten times more. So I'd like benchmarks to report success alongside cost, latency, and number of actions, so we can reason about the actual trade-offs.

The last thing I'd say is that benchmarks saturate quickly now, and contamination is a real concern. So I think we need more dynamic, continuously refreshed evaluations, and honestly more emphasis on evaluating agents in real deployment settings with human judgment in the loop, because ultimately the question is whether the agent is actually useful to the person relying on it.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks saturate quickly and calls for dynamic, continuously refreshed evaluations.

r002.rationale: It identifies distinct agent capabilities—trajectory quality, robustness, long-horizon performance, reliability, and efficiency—and describes measuring each with relevant criteria.

r003.rationale: It calls for measuring how performance degrades as task length grows and discusses tasks unfolding over hours or longer.

r004.rationale: It gives examples of real-world workflows, but does not propose building benchmarks from subproblems within those workflows.

r005.rationale: It does not propose using the difficulty of a workflow subproblem to define a benchmark challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that most of the benchmarks we have today were designed for a model that answers a question, and agentic systems don't really fit that mold. An agent is taking a sequence of actions in some environment, over many steps, with tools, with partial information, and often with a goal that's only loosely specified. So when we measure capability, we have to measure the whole trajectory, not just the final output.

A few things I'd want a good agentic benchmark to do. First, it should evaluate process, not only outcomes. Two agents can both get the right answer, but one of them got there by trying every possible action and the other reasoned its way there with a handful of well-chosen steps. Those are very different systems in terms of cost, safety, and reliability, and a benchmark that only checks the end state can't tell them apart.

Second, it needs to be interactive and stateful. A static dataset that you can memorize doesn't tell you much about how a model behaves when the environment responds to its actions, when a tool call fails, or when the plan it made in step two turns out to be wrong by step seven. Recovery from errors is actually one of the most important capabilities for an agent, and you only see it if the benchmark lets things go wrong.

Third, I'd push for long-horizon tasks that are decomposable. Real work is rarely a single call. It's "go read this codebase, figure out what's broken, fix it, verify the fix." If the benchmark is just a collection of short tasks stitched together, you miss the question of whether the model can hold a goal over a long context and keep track of what it's already done.

And then there's the reliability piece, which I think is underrated. For an agent, pass at one is not the interesting number. If I'm going to hand off a task and walk away, I care about pass at ten, or really, how consistently it succeeds across runs and across small perturbations of the task. A model that gets 80 percent on average but is wildly variable is much less useful than one that's a bit lower but predictable. So I'd like to see benchmarks report variance and robustness, not just a single headline score.

The last thing I'd say is that we should be careful about contamination and about what the benchmark actually incentivizes. Once a benchmark becomes the target, people optimize for it, and with agents that can mean the model learns the specific environment rather than the underlying skill. So the benchmarks need to be refreshed, they need held-out environments, and ideally they should be grounded in tasks that someone actually wants done, so that improving on the benchmark corresponds to improving on something real.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks become optimization targets, so they should be refreshed and use held-out environments. This communicates the recurring need for new benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It describes different dimensions of agent capability—process, interaction and recovery, long-horizon goal tracking, and reliability—and explains how benchmarks should measure them.

r003.rationale: It advocates long-horizon tasks and contrasts them with short tasks, but does not propose evaluating tasks across varying planning horizons.

r004.rationale: It gives a real-work workflow as an example of a long-horizon task, but does not propose constructing benchmarks from workflow subproblems.

r005.rationale: It does not use the difficulty of defining a workflow subproblem as a basis for designing a benchmark challenge.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to move beyond asking, “Did the model give the right answer?” and ask, “Could it actually complete the task?” For an agent, that might involve planning, using tools, observing what happened, and adjusting its approach when something doesn’t work.

So benchmarks need to capture that interaction over multiple steps. Can the model recover from a tool failure? Can it recognize that it’s missing information and ask for clarification? Does it know when to stop? You want to measure whether it achieved the goal, but also how reliably and efficiently it got there—how much time, computation, and human intervention it required.

And I think you need variation in the environment. If an agent succeeds only when everything looks exactly like the benchmark examples, that tells us relatively little about how useful it will be. The more interesting question is whether it can handle a slightly different task or an unexpected observation and still make progress. That’s where evaluation starts to get closer to the capabilities we actually want.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluation beyond right-answer scoring and varying environments, but does not mention benchmark saturation or a recurring need for new benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It names several agent behaviors and evaluation dimensions, but does not state that distinct capabilities need capability-specific measurement methods.

r003.rationale: It proposes multi-step interaction, but does not propose varying the length of planning horizons.

r004.rationale: It does not propose constructing benchmarks from subproblems in real workflows.

r005.rationale: It does not propose using the difficulty of defining a workflow subproblem to define a benchmark challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to move beyond measuring whether a model can answer an individual question correctly and look at whether it can accomplish a task over multiple steps. Can it plan, use tools, interpret the feedback it gets, and recover when something goes wrong?

For example, if an agent is working on a coding task, generating plausible code is only one part of the problem. Can it understand the repository, make the change, run the tests, and use the results to decide what to do next? The benchmark needs an environment where we can observe that whole process and verify the outcome.

And we should measure the resources required to get there—the number of interactions, the latency, the cost, and how much human intervention was needed. Reliability matters, too. An agent that succeeds once in ten attempts has a very different capability from one that consistently completes the task. So I would want benchmarks to capture successful outcomes, but also the conditions and constraints under which those outcomes are achieved.
